newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Pro-Indonesia youths pledge to support election.
newsitem.headline: Pro-Indonesia youths pledge to support election.

text.p: About 3,000 pro-government Indonesian youths said on Saturday they would support the May 29 general elections.

The pledge came amid calls from a number of student groups and activists for a poll boycott after Indonesian Democratic Party (PDI) leader Megawati Sukarnoputri was ousted at a government-backed congress last June.

The youths who were grouped in 39 organisations gathered at a ceremony organised by the National Committee of Indonesian Youths (KNPI) and led by Armed Forces Commander General Feisal Tanjung on Saturday.

"The Indonesian youths are ready to support the 1997 general elections...The Indonesian youth will actively participate in the elections and exercise their rights to vote," said the statement read out by Ali Masykur Musa, a representative of the youths.
The government-sanctioned KNPI is the umbrella of the country's youth organisations.
President Suharto last week asked the country's powerful armed forces to prevent any disturbances during next month's general election by those calling for a poll boycott.

"Please don't let this high political awareness be disturbed by those who are irresponsible and who want to lead the people astray by urging them not to use their right to vote," Suharto told the officers from the three wings of the military and the police.
"I ask the state security forces to prevent early every disturbance, blockage and threat to the general election, especially those to the security and safety of the nation," he said.

Voting is compulsory in Indonesia and voter turnout was about 95 percent at the last poll in 1992, but analysts from the ruling Golkar party estimate only about three percent of voters either deliberately spoiled their ballots or boycotted the poll.
Indonesia only allows Golkar, the Moslem-oriented United Development Party (PPP) and the Christian-Nationalist PDI to contest the elections.

With Indonesia's tightly controlled electoral system, Golkar is almost assured of achieving a landslide victory on May 29 and reaching its target of more than 70 percent of the vote, up from around 68 percent at the last poll.
The PPP won 17 percent and the PDI 15 percent in 1992.
